rationale: This is a very small (185 lines, 15 functions, ~2.1 KB text) compute-bound C++ benchmark whose core functions (eden, update, empty::next, living::sums) iterate over a 40x40 grid in hot loops, so runtime overhead tolerance must be kept low while correctness must be protected. SUB and SPLIT get the highest weights across the board because they are near-zero-cost transformations that safely increase instruction-level diversity and, in SPLIT's case, expose more basic blocks that amplify the obfuscating effect of any later-applied pass. FLA is given strong SecurityGain/DiversityGain (control-flow flattening is the highest-value structural defense against static analysis of these loop-heavy kernels) but depressed RuntimeCost and SizeCost tolerances, since flattening hot grid loops and inflating an already tiny binary are the main risks. BCF is kept as a secondary layer with moderate security value but low runtime tolerance, because bogus conditional branches execute repeatedly inside the simulation loops and this program has no slack for that. IBR, ICALL, and IGV are retained at moderate levels: they cheaply harden branch targets, call sites, and global references (life.cpp relies heavily on global/grid state, making IGV particularly effective here) without dominating the overhead budget, and their CorrectnessRisk weights are held below SUB/SPLIT because indirect transformations interact less predictably with C++ name mangling and vtable-style dispatch in code like this.
